# Systemic neglect hidden behind tolerance: the reproduction of vulnerability among aging heroin users within the community-based rehabilitation

**Authors:** Apei Song; Jiaojiao He; Zixi Liu

**Affiliations:** 1 School of Law, Society, and Criminology, University of New South Wales, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia | 2 School of Sociology and Anthropology, Xiamen University, Xiamen, Fujian, China | 3 School of Sociology and Anthropology, Xiamen University, Xiamen, Fujian, China

## Abstract

Contemporary Chinese drug governance is shifting its focus toward the rehabilitation of people who use drugs, prioritizing restorative over punitive measures. Moving beyond previous research that has primarily focused on the importance of community-based rehabilitation mechanisms in facilitating social reintegration, this study aimed to understand aging heroin users’ experiences within broader systems of power, citizenship, and social exclusion in China.

We conducted fieldwork in a city in the eastern region in China in 2020–2021 and interviewed 12 heroin users aged 65–75 years. We employed Atkinson’s life story interview as an approach to collect data and Abbott’s group life course to examine how aging heroin users, both as individuals and as a cohort with distinct drug experiences and aging traits, narrate their interactions within the national rehabilitation programs.

Our findings contend that older heroin users, even after testing positive, receive lenient institutional treatment, often exempting them from compulsory rehabilitation due to age-related health issues and care burdens. To mitigate the risk of overdose, drug enforcement authorities utilize social welfare programs as a means of promoting self-management among aging users. However, this approach neglects the general well-being needs of the older population. Moreover, drug social workers often overlook aging users as clients for their casework because of performance and tangling professional ethics. The systematic neglect thus formed, and it provokes reflection on the position of aging users and how they seek to be citizens but are excluded by the “violence of citizenship.”

We found the systematic neglect experienced by aging heroin users through the judicial process, welfare programs, and service practices. This structural disadvantage, more important than their needs, underscores the urgent value of addressing the social issues surrounding their marginalized position in society.

Keywords: Marginalization, Opioid use, Social inclusion, Violence of citizenship

This research elucidates the systemic neglect concealed beneath the guise of tolerance—nonincarceration and coercive control—as officials claim. Specifically, the combination of justice system exceptions, limited access to social welfare, and the omission of aging heroin users from casework services underscores the vulnerable social position of this demographic. By unveiling systemic neglect within current national rehabilitation programs, which display the “violence of citizenship,” this study advocates for rethinking structural drivers of their vulnerable positions and heightened awareness of the unique requirements of aging users and offers practical care assistance in overdoses.

## 

Intergenerational studies of substance use identify a specific “heroin generation” that was generally active in the late 20th and early 21st centuries. In the United States, this generation comprises those born between 1945 and 1954 who came of age during the 1960s and 1970s (Golub & Johnson, 1999; Hunt & Chambers, 1976). Today, many in this cohort are over the age of 70. In contrast, in China, the heroin generation emerged during the 1980s and 1990s, a period marked by significant social change and modernization, as people transitioned from stable careers, called “iron rice bowls,” to the pursuit of “freedom” or “wealth” (Bartlett, 2020; Li, 2024). This group, if they have not succumbed to overdose and infections acquired through unsafe injection practices, such as HIV or Hepatitis C and B, is generally over 55 years old today. Li (2024) further notes that this generation was the first group of people who used drugs to emerge after China declared itself a “drug-free nation” in 1952. Deeply entangled in the illicit heroin market that briefly flourished with economic reforms, they were not only ascribed the identity of people who use drugs but also that of drug dealers by Chinese law and social rules. Therefore, they are often stigmatized as greedy, nonmainstream, and desire-driven individuals, intersecting with the broader identities of criminals, transgressors, and members of subcultural groups.

Since 2008, the heroin generation has encountered a more institutionalized and systematic treatment process, primarily shaped by the Anti-Drug Law promulgated by the Chinese government in 2008 and the Drug Rehabilitation Regulations introduced in 2011. While contemporary drug policy continues to center on prohibition—a policy logic established since the 1990s—the rehabilitation turn has become increasingly pronounced (Song & Jiang, 2025). Currently, the national drug rehabilitation program in China operates through four models: compulsory isolation rehabilitation, community detoxification, community rehabilitation, and voluntary detoxification. The latter three fall under community-based rehabilitation, whereas compulsory isolation rehabilitation remains part of the ­government-led institutionalized model. In principle, the Chinese government offers voluntary detoxification as an option, whereby people sign agreements with drug rehabilitation service agencies to receive treatment. However, the effectiveness of this pathway remains limited, and most people who use drugs experience a rehabilitation trajectory that moves from institutionalized rehabilitation to community-based rehabilitation (Jiang & Song, 2025; Yang & Giummarra, 2021). Typically, this process begins with compulsory isolation rehabilitation administered by public security and judicial authorities, lasting approximately 2 years. Compulsory facilities resemble prison environments, where clients receive essential detoxification services while also being required to engage in labor and undergo moral corrections (Song et al., 2024). Once authorities determine that a person has successfully abstained from drugs in both behavior and intent, they are transferred to the community for a 3-year period of community rehabilitation, during which they remain under surveillance and risk assessment (Liu et al., 2016; Song & Liu, 2022). Notably, during the community-based rehabilitation phase, participants, including aging heroin users, may receive service support from drug social workers. This professional role is introduced into community-based rehabilitation through a government-purchased initiative. On the one hand, drug social workers assist the police with urine testing, consultations, and interviews; on the other, they deliver services designed to address the rehabilitation needs of participants (Song, 2024). This emerging supplementary focus is reflected in the Guidelines for Drug Control Social Work Services established in various regions, such as Xiamen’s Service Criteria (2024).

However, within the generalized model of drug rehabilitation, elders often follow a different path. Due to age-related health concerns, compulsory isolation rehabilitation centers (CIRC) have adopted a more cautious approach, frequently allowing older people to undergo rehabilitation within the community de facto. Nonetheless, this so-called lenient treatment may be overly optimistic and overlook ongoing challenges and complicated structural intentions. In recent years, several cities have proposed expanding the medical infrastructure and treatment capacity of CIRC to fully enforce the legal principle of “Yingguan Jinguan (management all if necessary),” ensuring that all individuals, regardless of age or health condition, remain subject to the “official” rehabilitation.

This back-and-forth of local policies and management reflects and perpetuates the underlying logic of citizenship violence embedded in China’s drug rehabilitation policy. Citizenship violence refers to the systematic deprivation and suppression of the legitimate social identity of people who use drugs by the state during governance (e.g., Campbell, 2020). This form of violence operates not only at the level of legal systems but also infiltrates everyday practices of governance. Criminologists have noted that, although China’s drug policy publicly emphasizes principles such as humanity, help, education, and people-orientation (Yiren weiben), in practice, it subjects people who use drugs to prolonged and repeated forms of supervision and control through both institutionalized rehabilitation and community-based systems (Li et al., 2022). In these processes, people who use drugs are frequently deprived of—or deliberately restricted from—basic rights afforded to other citizens, such as access to employment, freedom of movement, and even opportunities for their children’s promotions (Song & Liu, 2022). These exclusions create a vicious cycle of intergenerational marginalization under the guise of “correction.” The convergence of policy orientation with dominant urban management discourses exacerbates the identity dilemmas faced by people who use drugs. They are often positioned within a state of “suspended citizenship” (Song, 2024), wherein their civic status is neither fully recognized nor entirely revoked. Drug policy, therefore, functions not merely as a public health or social service initiative but as a governance tool through which the state redraws the boundary between “qualified citizens” and “dangerous others,” reinforcing legal and symbolic exclusion (Li, 2016). This form of citizenship violence manifests as a persistent contradiction within the Chinese rehabilitation system, which continuously oscillates between punitive control and welfare provision.

Within this context, management for aging heroin users is oversimplified. The complexity of substance use disorders among older populations becomes increasingly prominent as a critical aspect of their life course and a challenge for management. On the one hand, the physical functions of aging heroin users gradually deteriorate, and they are often afflicted by various diseases resulting from chronic or improper injection practices. Consequently, many seek opioids such as fentanyl, codeine, oxycodone, and tramadol to manage short-term pain relief. Unsurprisingly, some report underestimating the negative consequences of their alternative use (Ivsins et al., 2024), leading to emergencies and treatment assistance due to overuse. For example, a 2023 survey report on safe substance use among older adults, jointly conducted by Xinhuashe and the China Association of Geriatrics and titled “Looking for Sunny Elderly,” found that 44% of respondents had taken medication for chronic and geriatric diseases in the past 6 months and reported experiencing issues related to drug side effects and resistance. On the other hand, a growing body of public health scholarship has highlighted the rising number of opioid overdose deaths among individuals aged 65 and older over the past decade. The high incidence of overdose deaths among this group indicates that health care systems will face significant challenges in addressing their needs (Bonnie et al., 2019). Criminologists, similarly, have pointed out the rising costs and difficulties the correctional system will face in dealing with aging-related issues (Williams et al., 2012). These concerns are also reflected in China’s drug policies. According to the 2011 Drug Rehabilitation Regulations, “For those whose health conditions are no longer suitable for compulsory isolation and drug rehabilitation, the compulsory isolation treatment facilities should be changed to community rehabilitation.” However, in community settings, structural constraints remain evident. The 14th Five-Year Plan for the Development of National Aging Affairs and Elderly Care Service System, issued by the Chinese government, mandates that there should be at least one social worker for every 1,000 older adults. This extreme mismatch between demand and available resources has significantly increased the workload of social workers and neglected clients who are more problematic, intersecting with aging and a long history of substance use.

While these interdisciplinary and systemic critiques offer valuable insights into the trends concerning aging adults who use heroin, less focus has been given to their life stories as both individuals and members of substance use groups. There has been limited exploration of how they interact with present social dynamics and the events that shape their life experiences—essentially, influencing their thoughts, words, and actions today. Therefore, we use a life story approach to explore how aging users are experiencing and navigating structural forces and power dynamics behind these needs and to address the structural forces and power dynamics that explain why aging users remain vulnerable and constantly face identity issues.

This article will, therefore, provide a possible response by shifting the focus from the needs of older heroin users to the institutional and systemic frameworks that have consistently placed them at a disadvantage. By examining this framework of citizenship violence, we sought to understand why the broader older population, including aging heroin users, despite government attention, remains marginalized, and excluded. Specifically, we explore how aging heroin users in China, both as individuals and as a cohort with unique drug-use histories and aging-related challenges, narrate their interactions within the national rehabilitation programs. Through this analysis, we seek to uncover how power operates to define boundaries of citizenship, delineating who belongs to the category of “ourselves.” What is the situation of older heroin users within this framework, and how is their vulnerability explicitly caused by the processes of citizenship and its violence?

## Research design and methods

We used qualitative research in this study, interviewing people who inject/use Heroin and are over 65 years old. They have been enrolled in or completed community-based rehabilitation in a city in China anonymized as “M.” M, as an economically developed city in the eastern region, has a significant history of drug-related issues and structural events (Song, 2024), which led to the establishment of both institutionalized rehabilitation and community-based rehabilitation programs. This makes M representative of the broader experience of economically developed cities in China, attracting some drug scholars (Song & Jiang, 2025; Song & Liu, 2022).

Recruitment in M was primarily conducted through personal networks and expanded using a respondent-driven snowball sampling approach from 2020 to 2021. The first author’s experience conducting drug-related field research in M from 2018 provided an informal list of potential participants. The recruitment criteria for participants are 65 years or older; currently undergoing or having completed compulsory rehabilitation and community-based rehabilitation; currently using heroin or having used heroin within the past 3–4 years. We selected four participants as seeds from this list who met the initial communication and recruitment criteria based on their WeChat information and past field notes. They are Peter, Molly, Bill, and Hen. All of them met the research requirements, with attention given to diversity in gender, use of ways, welfare, and healthy conditions. Recruitment aligns with Li and colleagues’ (2022) proposal to use guanxi (relationships) to conduct research; thus, through the recommendations of seed-role participants, We completed interviews with 12 heroin users aged 65–75 years.

There are seven females and five males, four of whom were still using, five stopped using, and three were substituting other prescription drugs (two used morphine, and one used naloxone). Nine had at least one social welfare benefit, such as low-income, pension, or basic health insurance. Three of them had only a chronic illness (tracheitis, chronic pharyngitis, and rheumatoid), five had an acute illness (acute bronchitis, hepatitis C, and glaucoma), one had epilepsy, one had hemangioma, and two had HIV and continued to use drugs. Moreover, to enhance the credibility and validity of the results, we also employed data triangulation by conducting additional interviews with five social workers (service providers), two officials from the Narcotics Control Office, and three drug enforcement officers, thereby offsetting potential biases inherent in single-source studies.

The investigators conducted face-to-face interviews with participants. We provided formal informed consent to participants, and a verbal introduction of their rights and aims for this study was conducted before the interviews. We mostly conducted interviews lasting 30–70 min, using life story interviews (Atkinson, 1998) to cover the following topics: historical substance use experience, experience with law enforcement/criminal justice system/care system, recovery-oriented narratives, stigma feelings, family relationships, and strategies for self-care. It is worth noting that the interview process preferred to let participants express their formulation, storytelling content (Liu, 2018), and understanding of the life course of aging and opioid use intersecting. Every participant was offered one follow-up interview, allowing them time to reflect on and elaborate on the topics they did not cover in the first interview or raise vague questions that needed to be refined and expanded upon. All interviews were audio-recorded with their permission.

The life course serves as the dominant framework for data collection and analysis, focusing primarily on temporality (Baars, 1997, 2013) or “historicality” (Abbott, 2016). In substance use research, longitudinal empirical analysis of the onset, trajectories, turning points, and transitions in drug trafficking/use behaviors lies at the core of much of the field’s scholarship (Singer, 2005; Uggen & Thompson, 2003). Age is thus the primary variable commonly analyzed by the life course perspective to examine issues such as involvement, frequency, severity, duration, and cessation of offending or substance use (Blumstein 1986; Jiang, 2024). Beyond investigating individuals, we incorporate individual and group life histories from Abbott (2016) into the life course approach to connect past contingencies with present contexts, focusing on how early events shape structures and how behaviors continue to exert influence over time. Specifically, we analyze the life history narratives of aging heroin users, focusing on key interactional events—both past and present—to understand their engagement with the justice system, welfare institutions, and broader social structures, and to navigate their invisibility and circumvent systemic violence as members of a marginalized geriatric and substance-using group in an exclusionary civic framework.

For cleaning data, we processed the data in strict adherence to ethical standards and committed to maintaining the confidentiality of identifiable information to ensure participants’ privacy. We anonymized the names of participants and removed personal colloquialisms, catchphrases, and some sentences they said to describe their appearance and characteristics during the translation process. In the data analysis process, we coded stories and events adhered to a timeline covering the 1990s, the early 21st century, and the present. This allowed us to trace significant life course events among interviewees. Simultaneously, we consciously distinguished events at individual and group levels, editing the temporality of their experiences using a narrative approach to emphasize interactions.

Returning to our central research question—examining the structural position of older heroin users within the current policy climate, shaped by recovery-oriented frameworks, and aging trends—we categorized key periods and events in greater depth. Through this process, we identified and ideal-typed commonalities and differences. Ultimately, by integrating structural shifts in rehabilitation policy with personal life experiences, three primary themes emerged: (a) the “exception” to the criminal justice system at the compulsory treatment stage; (b) “specialization” within social welfare at the community rehabilitation stage; and (c) “deliberate non-selection” in social work services at the self-rehabilitation stage. These themes illuminate the life course of older heroin users as they move from compulsory isolation treatment to community rehabilitation and ultimately to self-rehabilitation, underscoring their continuous exclusion at each stage and diversity of neglect. Moreover, they also unfold the relationships between systematic neglect and citizenship violence, exposing the structural limitations inherent in becoming (or being denied) a “good identity.”

## Results

### The “exception” to the criminal system at the compulsory rehabilitation stage: unburdened capacity and instrumentalized ties

All participants, when they were younger (generally before 50 years old), had compulsory rehabilitation experiences in CIRC (Li, 2024), which detained them for coercive control for an average of 8–9 years. CIRC, as incarcerated sites of power performance, have far fewer therapeutic responsibilities than disciplinary ones—shaping moral norms and a commitment to physical well-being, which become essential conditions for release (Song et al., 2024). As they age, the participants’ physical illness issues become more prominent, particularly acute diseases. This puts justice venues with limited treatment and care capacity at risk of inadvertently assuming unplanned medical responsibilities, thereby increasing the stigma associated with incarcerated deaths. Therefore, justice workers in M city have adopted a practice of “lenience,” allowing aging users who test positive for substance use to undergo mandatory treatment in community settings rather than institutional incarceration. Participant Peter had a similar experience and noted that this nonincarcerated tolerance, in fact, reflects the structural contradictions within the system, specifically, the tension between limited institutional capacity for medical care and the growing health needs of aging users. This lenience, while intended to address medical vulnerabilities, inadvertently creates challenges for community-level policing frameworks. Such trade-offs highlight how operational adjustments in one subsystem (justice) can expose structural gaps in another (community care), rather than reflecting “helplessness” of the system itself.

I tested positive last month, I’m in my 60s, I am diabetic, and I’ve had an acute myocardial infarction (AMI) before. They know they cannot put me into a CIRC. I had to take medication regularly, test my blood sugar, and recheck my body; many troubles I brought to them. So, the police can only scare me, maybe detain me for a while or keep an eye on my neighbourhood. (Peter, 20200714)

However, behind the so-called leniency, not being subjected to coercive control and imprisonment, is not only the weakening of the shocking and punitive nature of the drug-testing and coercive model but also the neglect of the older population. As Chinese substance use disorders have been gradually alleviated in recent years, urban anti-drug agencies have been modified in their mandates, which has had a significant impact on the professional development and outcomes of drug police and anti-drug justice workers. Thus, participant Lily told her story of being talked to and bribed to help fulfil the justice and public security targets. Rather than reinforcing justice, she felt that such practices fostered corruption and formalism, undermining the integrity of drug enforcement efforts, yet she did so in exchange for nonincarceration.

In 2023, I’m at home. My legs are wrong; I would also ask my social worker to get me some legal prescription drugs with morphine, ephedrine, as the insomnia was too bad. Police Officer A later tested me for drugs, and it was positive for sure. Police Officer A and I agreed to cooperate; he would help me to instruct the social worker and the doctor to ensure that I was given a steady supply of prescription medication while I made a trip to the CIRC to fulfil the lower target. Because of my health issues, I was released back into the community for rehabilitation in less than a month. (Lily, 20210407)

Another connotation of this exception lies in the more dynamic relationships between aging heroin users and the criminal system. Compared to other age groups who use drugs, responders with overlapping intersecting elements of illness, substance use, and old age derive a causal relationship with police and justice workers who jointly conspire to fulfil the sectional constraints of the criminal system. They made rational use of legitimate institutional regulations to not only accomplish what was required in the rules but also exploited the loopholes in the rules to maximize the rights of both parties. Similarly, the mixing of Lily’s prescription drugs and heroin, and whether it had the potential for overdose and abuse to threaten their health, did not receive special attention from the judicial process.

Aging users are treated differently by the justice system and are not able to be compulsorily rehabilitated, which is, in fact, a blessing and a curse. The criminal system considers the care of the special needs and physical problems of older adults but directly assigns the duty of specialized services (like social workers), as well as pushing them out of the law enforcement scope in the name of tolerance. This is reasonable because of the result of renegotiation between criminality and society, realigning with the scope of power and responsibility. However, beyond judicial neglect, there is no provision for any underpinning, targeted, compensatory law enforcement measures. One of the interlocutors, Den, emphasized, “It’s just a de facto behavior, not a rule, so it depends on which police officer you communicate with. How your treatment is arranged depends on the individual. It’s still very unstable.” This highlights the discretionary nature of drug enforcement. Another participant, Lily, expressed a more radical perspective: “No one, even policing, cares about you anyway. It’s the same whether you use drugs or not. When you get older, you are less of a threat to society.” This has undoubtedly contributed to a more remarkable disregard for heroin use among older users on the one hand, and to a system of anti-drug governance that sees aging users as a political resource to be manipulated at will on the other (Jiang & Song, 2025). Ultimately, the exception position, in effect, creates an awkward position between the promise of treatment and political expectations.

### “Specialization” in social welfare at community-based rehabilitation stage: labeling and threshold setting

The community-based rehabilitation stage has become a predominant rehabilitation model for aging heroin users in recent years. Typically, individuals sign a community drug rehabilitation agreement, committing to supervision, regular urine testing, and reporting their movements. Following this, a community correction or assistance team informs them about available social welfare programs and policy benefits. However, older heroin users often find that despite the shift away from institutional confinement, the stigma associated with substance use persists. The continued labeling of substance use has been perpetuated by aging people, who have been blamed for heroin use from the 1980s until the present day. Criminologist Li (2024) describes this as “lost on the road to prosperity” to seek to re-navigate their misunderstanding. Nevertheless, for management and the public consciousness, an overemphasis on the past at the expense of the present remains the norm. Their patient and victim performance has been hidden in the shadow of the labels of lawbreakers and offenders, resulting in chronic neglect of social welfare rights and interests (Song & Liu, 2022). The structural tolerance of older adult care and welfare coverage is fragmented by personal experiences of substance use, and older heroin users are thus placed in a black box of social welfare distribution.

Aging with heroin use generally faces challenges with pain management. In addition to using heroin to manage pain, 90% of drug reimbursement and easy access to medications through Medicare and Medicaid have been how this group has built a network of alternative medications to maintain pain relief. Sixty-three-year-old Bill describes how he legally obtains alternative drugs to combat physiological pain through the older adult’s benefit program:

I would drink heavily, and no one cared how much I bought. With other (legal) prescription drugs, I have health insurance and can pick up the amount I need; the doctor tells me to take the drugs as prescribed, which I do. But I am not sure what happens when I mix it with heroin, but I try not to take them together. (Bill, 20200704)

Such risky maneuvers further exacerbate the stereotypes of communities and civic authorities who set an invisible threshold for benefit claims. They consider whether aging people will abuse the tolerance and charity of the healthcare system to do something detrimental to their health. This threshold, labeled as a safety precaution, is logically combined with the “stopping use of drug (Jiedu)” policy of requiring older applicants with “previous convictions” to actively participate in urine testing, with positive tests leading to the suspension of benefits. The interviewee, Den, was outraged by this invisible design:

I applied with other elders, and they immediately asked me to do a urine test because of my heroin use 15 years ago, and the secret I had kept all my life was instantly exposed. All my friends knew at once. I was a compliant applicant, I paid my taxes, I worked hard, and although I ended up with a pension place, I was humiliated again by the process. (Den, 20200805)

Even universal welfare benefits become context-specific bargaining chips for older heroin users. Two cases from our interviews highlight this situation where they are unwillingly governed but are forced to comply in exchange for welfare resources. Noam, 57, has an eye disability that prevents him from travelling to a community hospital to receive routine medical supplies for the management of a chronic condition. The police then asked Noam to provide a urine test report to contribute to the indicator despite having completed the compulsory rehabilitation process. In exchange, the Narcotics Control institution, in collaboration with the community, arranged for a social worker to assist him in collecting his medication and purchasing household items. The second case is similar. Bob, 62, who took an unauthorized break from a community-based treatment program during the pandemic, subsequently entered into a partnership with the drug police to claim his pension, whereby he was apprehended, filed a case, and urine tested for drugs in exchange for remaining rehabilitated in the community and claiming his pension. These embodied stories thus show that, in daily life, tolerant welfare policies are not unconditionally implemented for the group of aging heroin users.

### “Deliberate non-selection” in social work services at the self-rehabilitation stage: performances and tangling professional ethics

The self-rehabilitation stage, often framed as Huiguishehui (social reintegration) in government discourse, is designed to support individuals transitioning out of community rehabilitation programs or seeking broader social integration. To facilitate this process, the government procures social work services to address diverse client needs. However, in practice, Participant Yun has observed that “some social workers frequently avoid establishing formal case relationships with us.” This reluctance is shaped by an awareness of the social heterogeneity of potential caseloads and the performance expectations of their organizations. For instance, Participant Hen voluntarily sought assistance from a social worker to obtain HIV antiretroviral medication—a request that did not align neatly with conventional service frameworks. This highlights the limitations of the existing support system, where structural constraints and institutional priorities influence the extent and nature of care provided to aging users.

The skin on my arms was very uncomfortable, and it was worse when I got wet…ashamed to be like this, and I’m afraid to go to the local health center to collect my HIV antiretrovirals, it’s too obvious. So, I tried to ask the social workers to collect it for me, but they were not very willing and always busy… The pain, it’s always with me, and the fentanyl is my antidote, in this empty room. (Hen, 20210623)

This situation might be because the administrative district where Hen resides employs only two social workers. These social workers were initially tasked with supporting 34 clients in community-based rehabilitation, 17 of whom were over 50, and 12 were over 65. However, with a shift in the performance evaluation criteria for anti-drug authorities, they were subsequently required to conduct at least one household visit per year with the entire population of 432 individuals who had a history of substance use. The purpose of these visits was to understand the individuals’ basic circumstances and assess the risk of relapsing into substance use. Despite this significant expansion of their caseload, social workers’ annual service targets remained unchanged, leaving them responsible for completing seven casework and three group assignments. This adjustment in micro-level enforcement and management procedures has placed increased pressure on social workers. Mimi, the social worker who had previously assisted Hen, shared her experience of the growing pressure with investigators, emphasizing “the plenty of challenges of working under such conditions” (Mimi, 20210423). Other social worker interlocutors also noted that authorities often perceive providing services to older heroin users as a waste of resources. There is a reluctance to allow service providers to become overly involved, as this is seen as placing an additional burden on the government. Yong recounted:

You see, an elderly heroin user was diagnosed with cancer. A social worker from our agency supported him until the end. Others offered him banners as a sign of recognition, but he refused them—he did not want such displays of support. However, the community leaders needed them. They visited him, wrote press releases, and publicized their involvement. In the end, after he passed away, no one cared. The leader of the Narcotics Control Office even considered it unlucky. He was displeased that he had just visited the man before his death. So, he said, “Don’t help those who are too close to be dying in the future.” That’s exactly what he said. His death was seen as a relief—by the community, the police station, and the local administration—because one less person meant one less name on their list. (Yong, 20210507)

Moreover, professional ethics and goals within social work also contribute to this sense of “non-selection.” Core professional values such as acceptance and respect (Kirzner & Miserandino, 2023) are challenging to apply when building relationships with older heroin users. Participant Tin highlighted this disconnect, stating:

Who would genuinely accept me? The last Kang social worker who came didn’t accept me at all. Don’t pay attention to what’s said, look at what’s done. I have a Kwan Kung statue1 and a tattoo in my house, and he was scared. He came to serve me, but he couldn’t wait to get out of there. (Tin, 20220827)

Additionally, fostering and upholding the participants’ capacity for self-determination (Spicker, 1990) remains a significant challenge. Participant Ben, a 73-year-old heroin user who is now on morphine substitution, exemplifies this struggle. After multiple mandatory detoxifications and the onset of senility, Ben has become socially disconnected over time. Despite these challenges, he remains an active learner, persistently striving for self-determination. He approaches his gradual social exclusion with dignity, seeking to maintain his independence while making efforts not to burden others.

It’s hard. I’m alone. I’ve been living in this community for 15 years now. For 15 years, I relied on the relationships I had built with a few other drug users in the beginning—we helped and supported each other. Then some of them died from alcoholism, and others from illness. I went from having support to being alone. That’s when I got a dog. I learned to use my mobile phone, order takeaways, and use Alipay. Huang, my social worker, taught me. He felt that as long as I stayed on morphine and my dependency remained unchanged, society would never truly accept me. But I knew that 15 years ago—I accepted that society wouldn’t accept me. I just wanted to eat what I wanted and socialize with whoever I wanted. (Ben, 20210513)

Ben, the oldest participant, exuded a sense of calm and reflection, showing the depth of a man who has traversed a lifetime of aging, substance use, moments of brilliance, and periods of despondency. He represented a rare kind of interviewee, someone who had come to terms with his past and present. While Huang, his social worker, expressed frustration, feeling that her efforts were in vain. She wanted Ben to adopt healthier habits and develop the ability to make entirely rational decisions. This desire is rooted in the structure of caseworker self-determination (Biestek, 1961): the right to self-determination should be limited to clients who have the capacity to make positive and constructive choices, aligned with civil law and morality. In Ben’s case, however, the choices he wished to make, though outside this conventional framework, were peaceful and brought him a sense of comfort. While they may not have aligned with Huang’s expectations or the ethical standards typically applied in social work, Ben’s decisions reflected his personal reconciliation with his life, illustrating a more complex, individualized form of self-determination.

Although social workers were not able to fully support participants in reclaiming their “good” citizenship or reintegrating into society, aging users still acknowledged the humanitarian value of some social workers’ efforts. Participant Hen remarked, “Sometimes, I would rather ask social workers for help than my own children. For example, social workers don’t refuse to help me with things like unclogging sewers or picking up items. They deliver them to my home very quickly.” As frontline actors with direct and sustained contact with people who use drugs, social workers themselves also expressed doubts and reflections regarding the effectiveness of current national rehabilitation programs. However, deeply embedded within government-purchased and policy-driven rehabilitation projects, they often resorted to political discourse to rationalize systemic shortcomings. Ultimately, care providers reproduce existing power dynamics through what might be described as “micro-resistance, real reinforcement.” Social worker Zhao’s comments illustrate this dynamic contradiction:

In daily contact, we know that elderly drug users are not harmful—they’re just ordinary older people in need of care. But they also need to take responsibility for what they’ve done in the past. Government supervision is necessary. After all, they’re people with low credibility. Who knows if they’re lying or just performing? So, I’m happy to help them with their daily needs, but I’m also happy to help the government keep an eye on them. (Zhao, 20210507)

In sum, while specialized social work services may not have deliberately excluded older heroin users from the outset, the constraints of external project-based funding models and power dynamics often lead social workers to make rational choices that prioritize meeting performance criteria. Additionally, within the framework of professional ethics and morality, social workers—due to their subjective interpretations and acceptance of cultural challenges—gradually adopt a detached approach toward groups grappling with the complex intersections of substance use, aging, and illness. But at the very least, their care introduces the possibility, allowing for moments of micro-level, dynamic flexibility within an otherwise controlled structure.

## Discussion: reimagining “be citizens and ourselves” from a neglect-citizenship violence perspective

The exclusion and neglect experienced by older heroin users can be understood as a form of “natural” marginalization, occurring subtly yet systematically. Community workers and drug enforcement authorities often, albeit with a degree of detachment, engage in practices that easily dismiss or overlook this population. This process highlights how societal preferences emerge, where certain groups are deemed worthy of attention while others are relegated to the periphery. The question arises based on participants’ common inquiry when we interviewed, “Are we the same? How can I be accepted again and become a normal person?” These sensitive concerns, in fact, refer to those who are the favored members of society and who are considered outcasts. Moreover, the life courses of participants again highlighted how these social divisions not only materialize but also become deeply ingrained within our social consciousness and personal identities. In responding to these melancholic questions from clients, one must consider how such marginalized groups, like older heroin users, are continually reshaped, expanding, or shrinking based on fluctuating societal and institutional priorities.

To fully grasp these dynamics, it may be necessary to revisit Foucault’s essay in 1984, What is Enlightenment, where he discusses how the construction of the “ourselves” is intertwined with broader structures of power and knowledge. Foucault provides a framework for critiquing our thoughts, actions, and existence through what he terms a “historical ontology of ourselves.” He highlights the contingency that has shaped us into “what we are,” as well as the potential to no longer be, do, or think in the same ways we currently do (Foucault, 1984, p. 45). This critical stance seeks to expand, as broadly as possible, the continuous and undefined pursuit of freedom. Structural factors, including knowledge, power, and moral norms, profoundly influence the formation of our identities. In our research, this knowledge-power system is represented by neglect. Simultaneously, this formation is marked by its contingency, with Foucault’s historical analysis shedding light on the boundaries and specificities that define certain groups or individuals. Those who find themselves on the other side of contemporary moral boundaries—the “contemporary limits of the necessary” (p. 43)—were once considered part of us, yet now stand apart, illustrating the dynamic and constructed nature of social divisions. Based on these ideas, I will explain how systemic neglect has embedded forms of citizenship violence and how contingency is reflected in the shifting expressions of citizenship among the aging heroin-using community. They are working together to shape and also reflect aging users’ reimagination of “be citizens and ourselves.”

Our findings highlight that systematic neglect, for marginalized and multiply vulnerable older heroin users, represents a tacit endorsement and reinforcement of citizenship violence. First, neglect is a consequence of citizenship-violence-based policies (e.g., Paiva et al., 2010). Practices such as compulsory isolation and dynamic monitoring within community-based rehabilitation reinforce the stigma that frames people who use drugs as unclean, untrustworthy, and inherently risky. Law enforcement agencies promote slogans like “don’t associate with drug users” and “say no to drugs,” constructing participants as socially dangerous and thereby undermining their ability to maintain ordinary interpersonal networks. This framing pushes them further away from institutionally recognized lifestyles, rendering them invisible in public life. Second, neglect functions as a reproduction mechanism of citizenship violence. By disregarding the needs and rights of participants, state institutions, including compulsory isolation centers, do not merely exclude them from social participation but also absolve themselves of responsibility. Rehabilitation becomes reduced to routine assessment procedures, and care responsibilities are offloaded to social workers in a bureaucratically convenient but ultimately collusive manner. This process not only diminishes administrative risk but also masks systemic disengagement as policy compliance. Finally, neglect operates as a daily modality through which citizenship violence is enacted. The state’s deliberate inattention filters downward through bureaucratic hierarchies, shaping community-level attitudes, and reinforcing stigma. This results in the erosion of familial and neighborhood ties, leaving participants estranged from kinship networks, community life, and everyday social belonging. Their civic identity becomes deeply stigmatized, leading to exclusion not only from formal institutions but also from informal self-identified communities, resulting in a profound disconnection from all forms of collective life.

However, when the shifting identities of participants are situated within the broader state-society relationship, it becomes evident that the choices made by these older heroin users, especially heroin use, are not purely the result of personal agency but rather manifestations of contingency shaped by broader social transformations. Aging people who used heroin during the period of China’s market economy reform (in the 1980s) were a group of people who dared to change from a stable iron rice bowl (Bartlett, 2020) to the construction of a market economy. At that time, reform and opening up as a policy was a contingency for the socialist political system. It was also a contingency that the participants happened to be within the scope of the special economic zone, and a contingency that they chose to try a new career. The boundaries of “ourselves” drawn by the social forces of knowledge, power, and morality at that time never considered drug problems such as heroin use. Therefore, they were also “ours” and the darlings of social development at that time. Some participants still benefit from this today. Although Ben and Helen are nearly 70 years old, they still rely on the rent they bought in the center of M city to pay for their expenses. Ben noted that “To some extent, we are now excluded, yet in the past, we were sought after. This is the Waterloo and the drama of life (20210703).” Today, however, substance use positions them within three intersecting negative contexts as not “us”: political oppression, cultural stigma, and labor force marginalization. Interlocutor Lily keenly emphasized, “The root of feeling excluded is the sense that I am different from everyone else and subject to discrimination. While this discrimination looks like occurring in small relationships, but I just tell you, it is a matter of social propaganda or legal frameworks (20210621).” From this, they experience systematic neglect across judicial processes, welfare programs, and service provision practices.

Rehabilitation policies are implemented with “tolerance” toward older heroin users, which is solely a commitment not to incarcerate them when using drugs. However, this condescending expression is, in fact, fueled by the older population’s unique “vulnerabilities,” issues of disease and pain, because of the never-formal announcement. This so-called tolerance is followed by systematic neglect, taking root in the citizenship violence. Narratives like “I want to be a citizen” (Ben, 20210513) echo Deslandes et al.’s (2022) critique of colonial frameworks. Noncitizen exclusion itself can also be understood as a form of citizenship violence—a mechanism that systematically denies complete social belonging to those marked by criminalization and past substance use. Ordinary groups barely feel the violence of citizenship. However, for marginalized groups, how they are classified as citizens by the state, the “ourselves,” is direct, radical, and structural violence. The ups and downs of this violence are recounted in the life stories of aging heroin users. Economic transition puts them in the “political spotlight” (Hen, 20210623), and their contingency experience of opioid use brings them “down from the forefront of social necessity” (Bill, 20200705), and even into the danger of “losing our autonomy” (Peter, 20200716), due to the harshness of drug-related crime in the 21st century. If we go back to the original scene of heroin use, contingency has been playing out ever since, yet only this time, they are on the outside as we reconfigure the boundaries of the “ourselves” of the new world. The ideal citizen, in the present, points, at least in part, to the healthy, laboring, procreative traits (Rose, 2010) that are alien to older heroin users, and, to be honest, no one can be sure at all times that they do not have any tensions of identity, because society’s “Qianjin yundong (forward movement)” and “priorities” are always relative and changeable in the broad context of genealogy and history.

Finally, it is worth noting that the presence of “violence of citizenship” as a framing of harm-making in aging care is often overshadowed by the politics of tolerance, benevolence, and lowered moral stance. Scholarship in aging care and elders who use opioids points to the high level of attention and special resources provided and invested by the government and society in serving older adults (Barrett & Barbee, 2017). Thus, age as a key dimension of institution, performance, and identity will reproduce age inequality (Calasanti, 2003; Barrett, 2022). In contrast to other forms of inequality, which can be eliminated by refusing to recognize the existence of social categories, inequality in old age, like a point to be reached, a journey for everyone, will be difficult to eliminate in terms of group categories, but is a product of interactions destined to be reproduced repeatedly. Participant Peter reflected that age itself might be a factor in the heightened sense of violence, noting, “Perhaps it is because of our age that we feel more excluded and have withdrawn from mainstream society. In this way, we face greater discrimination than other elderly individuals, yet older people in general are more marginalized than the young.” Moreover, the way in which the ideology of age distinguishes “ourselves,” the difference between youth and old age (Katz & Calasanti, 2014) and associates it with the positive and negative aspects of health, is consistently related to the process of socially constructed citizenship, whereby the ideal citizen is, at least in part, directed toward the productive advantages. The empirical research in this article points to how identities at the intersection of age and substance use render participants systematically invisible, and the truths of their rationale for heroin use, their personal needs, and their disempowerment are deliberately disregarded and set aside, all of which occurs in the context of the official promise of a tolerant discourse—you will not be forced to be detoxified and coercive controlled.

## Conclusion

We found that within the organizational framework of contemporary drug policy, older heroin users appear to be treated leniently—exempt from compulsory control even after testing positive. However, in practice, they are systematically neglected by national rehabilitation programs. This includes being treated as exceptions by the judicial system, receiving special positions in the welfare system, and being the “deliberate non-selection” by social workers. Then, we note that the “systemic neglect” that participants are dimly aware of nourishes violence of citizenship, forming the differences between the identity of age and opioid use intersection and ideal citizenship. This shapes a mechanism of age inequality that goes beyond the superficial issue of so-called needs and resources and is deeply rooted in the workings of power. By unveiling systemic neglect within current government-promoted rehabilitation models, this study advocates for heightened awareness of the equality of aging users and offers practical care assistance, especially in overdoses. Future research on this topic would benefit from the systematic and dynamic explanation of diverse neglect and citizenship-caused harms that might shed light on effective strategies for real change of their disadvantage.
